newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians begin voting in critical post-war poll.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians begin voting in critical post-war poll.

text.p: Bosnia's critical post-war elections began on Saturday with more than 4,000 polling stations opening their doors across the country.
Many refugees waiting to vote held out scant hope that the elections, laid out in the Dayton peace treaty which ended 43 months of war, would help forge a unified Bosnia.
One elderly Serb refugee from Sarajevo who had come from Belgrade to vote in Serb-held eastern Bosnia said the outcome was predictable.
"Everyone's going to vote for their own family," he said in a reference to the nationalist parties that led the ethnic factions through the war.
Many elderly refugees who had voted in Sarajevo within half an hour of the polls opening had tears in their eyes. They told reporters they hoped the vote would mean they could soon go home.

The United States has led a chorus of senior Western officials in publicly proclaiming the country has no choice but to go through with the elections, however flawed, if it is ever to recover from the conflict.
The American envoy who beat out the Dayton peace accord, Richard Holbrooke, leads a U.S. presidential delegation observing the elections.
Far from ratifying the territorial divisions forged in war, Holbrooke declared the poll would pave the way for the next stage in the peace process -- the creation of central government structures.
"The Dayton agreement does not provide for secession. We are opposed to that and we all agree that that is not what this election is all about," he told reporters.

But secession has been a consistent theme of the campaigns for the leading Serb and Croat parties. The ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) in particular has made no secret of its desire to cut its territory away from Bosnia and graft it to neighbouring Serbia.

Even when election organisers forced her to publicly denounce such rhetoric on local television, acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic used her delivery to make it clear she was committed to Bosnia's division.

One elderly Serb refugee was heard saying to a friend outside a polling station in Vlasenica in eastern Bosnia: "I agree. All (Moslems) should be exterminated for good. We didn't fight this bloody war so Moslems could vote in Bosnia."
The biggest short-term fear of the international community was of violence between ethnic rivals as they meet on Saturday in places they once fought over.
Hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced people were expected to travel rough roads in the journey back to the home towns they fled during the war.

To make sure the mass movement of people passes off peacefully, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the NATO-led peacekeeping force have drawn up an elaborate security plan that directs voters along 19 "secure" routes across ethnic boundary lines.

Almost every one of the 60,000 peacekeepers will be on duty to snuff out any hint of trouble before it flares out of control. But there will still be roughly twice as many polling stations as OSCE observers.

In a final appeal for peace, U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez, who commands the NATO force, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, and Robert Frowick, overseeing the elections as regional OSCE director, issued a joint statement.

"We urge you all to approach election day with dignity, to consider your own choice carefully, and to know that your vote is a secret vote," they urged Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats, who have scant experience with democracy.
